title: Beliefs & Foundations
description: Little Muslim → Pro. Short questions for children ready to connect familiar Islamic beliefs with simple explanations and everyday choices. Covers the six foundations of iman, ihsan, five pillars, faith and good actions, intentions, taqwa, personal responsibility, hope and repentance, angels, Iblis, earlier scriptures, the universal prophetic message, knowledge of the unseen, just judgment, Paradise, small deeds, hearts and actions, life as a test, decree with responsible effort, and cooperation with reliance on Allah. An adult may read questions aloud or explain unfamiliar words. All questions are Pro level within the Kids audience.
levelMethod: Pro is the highest editorial level within Little Muslim, not the Educated User level. It emphasizes connecting familiar ideas, distinguishing a teaching from a common misconception, completing simple sets and applying beliefs to short situations. All three question styles remain at Kids Pro level; styles are not difficulty levels. No specialist theology debates, detailed legal rulings, obscure historical facts, Arabic grammatical analysis or memorization of reference numbers is required. Level has not been calibrated with children's reading or response data. Quiz performance describes learning needs, not a child's faith or worth.

review.referenceCheck: Linked Quran passages and reports from Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim checked during preparation. Questions and explanations are original child-friendly educational paraphrases, not verbatim translations. Present-day situations illustrate applications; they are not events narrated in the cited reports. The six foundations follow the answer about iman in the hadith of Jibril; the five pillars follow the separate foundations report. These learning sets are not used to claim that faith and action are unrelated, or to judge someone's religious status. Ihsan is explained through awareness that Allah sees the worshipper, without asking children to imagine Allah's appearance. Intention examples explain that purposes can differ without allowing children to read another person's heart or making a good intention justify harm. Taqwa, hearts, deeds and the promise of Paradise are taught without ranking classmates' hidden faith, judging clothing or wealth, or deciding a particular person's final destiny. Personal responsibility is not inherited guilt; it does not excuse one's own participation in another person's wrongdoing. Children are not assigned all adult legal responsibilities. Hope in mercy is paired with sincere return and improvement rather than despair or permission to persist in harm. Angels are distinguished from divinity, and Iblis is identified as a jinn without invented unseen details or frightening storytelling. Earlier scriptures are identified only as named in the cited verses. The universal message is distinguished from language fluency, and no group is invited to mistreat another. Independent knowledge of the unseen belongs to Allah; the second Quran reference preserves the distinction that He may disclose unseen knowledge to chosen messengers. This is not a prohibition on ordinary evidence-based planning or forecasting. Judgment and small deeds are discussed without graphic punishment, obsessive checking of thoughts, or equating every accident with deliberate wrongdoing. The verse about life's test is not used to treat academic scores, illness, hardship or prosperity as proof of someone's faith or Allah's rejection. Accepting decree is compatible with learning, taking responsibility and seeking suitable help; it does not justify blaming an innocent person or refusing needed support. Ordinary cooperation with teachers and other people is distinguished from worship, without making every request for help permissible regardless of its purpose. Dangerous objects should be handled by suitable adults. This is not independent scholarly approval or a completed review with children.

selectionHints.unknownResponse: Use I am not sure as a separate UI action, not a fifth option.

questions.question: Which list matches the six foundations of iman in the hadith of Jibril?

options.text: Allah, angels, scriptures, messengers, the Last Day and divine decree
Prayer, fasting, Hajj, trade, travel and language
Angels, seasons, colors, games, clothing and food
Wealth, fame, strength, beauty, ancestry and popularity

questions.explanation: The report names six foundations of belief, including Allah's decree concerning good and bad. These are not a list of school subjects or possessions.

questions.question: What does ihsan teach us to remember during worship?

options.text: Other people's applause is the purpose of worship
Allah sees us, even though we do not see Him
Worship matters only when a teacher watches
The fastest worship is always the most sincere

questions.explanation: Ihsan concerns worship with deep awareness of Allah. The hadith teaches remembering that He sees us, rather than performing for an audience.

questions.question: Which list names the five pillars taught in the hadith?

options.text: Prayer, drawing, running, sleep and trade
Angels, books, messengers, colors and seasons
Shahadah, salah, zakat, Ramadan fasting and Hajj
Wealth, clothing, fame, prizes and travel

questions.explanation: The five pillars are central foundations of Islam. Learning their names does not mean every child immediately has all an adult's duties.

questions.question: What does the hadith include among the branches of faith?

options.text: Winning every argument about religion
Having the most expensive belongings
Being praised by every person nearby
Removing something harmful from a path

questions.explanation: The report connects faith with speech, modesty and useful action. Safe care for others can express what we learn about belief.

questions.question: According to the hadith about intentions, what matters in evaluating a deed?

options.text: The purpose for which a person does it
Only how many people notice it
Only how expensive it looks
Only whether it becomes popular

questions.explanation: The hadith connects deeds with intentions. Two outwardly similar actions can be done for different purposes.

questions.question: What does the Quran connect honor before Allah with?

options.text: Belonging to the richest family
Taqwa: being mindful of Allah and seeking to obey Him
Speaking the most popular language
Having the largest social following

questions.explanation: The verse gives importance to righteousness, not ancestry or status. It does not ask us to rank classmates' hidden faith.

questions.question: What does the Quran teach about carrying someone else's burden of sin?

options.text: Children automatically inherit every relative's wrongdoing
A family name makes every action blameworthy
One person does not carry another person's sin
An innocent person must take someone else's moral blame

questions.explanation: The verse teaches personal responsibility. Being related to someone does not make us guilty of their wrongdoing.

questions.question: Which response joins the Quran's teaching about mercy with returning to Allah?

options.text: Give up all hope after any mistake
Use mercy as permission to keep hurting people
Pretend our choices never need improvement
Keep hope in Allah's mercy and turn back sincerely

questions.explanation: The verses bring hope and repentance together. Allah's mercy encourages returning to Him, rather than despair or deliberate persistence in harm.

questions.question: How do these Quranic verses describe angels in relation to Allah?

options.text: Honored servants who act at His command
Gods who share His right to worship
Beings who make Allah obey them
Children who supply what Allah lacks

questions.explanation: Angels are honored servants, not partners in Allah's divinity. Believing in them is different from worshipping them.

questions.question: Which group does the Quran identify Iblis as belonging to?

options.text: The human prophets
The jinn
The people of Makkah
The recording angels

questions.explanation: The Quran explicitly says Iblis was one of the jinn. Stories should follow that teaching rather than inventing a different identity.

questions.question: Which two prophets' earlier scriptures are named at the end of Al-Ala?

options.text: Yusuf and Yunus
Dawud and Sulayman
Ibrahim and Musa
Zakariyya and Yahya

questions.explanation: These verses mention the scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa. Revelation did not begin only with the Quran's arrival.

questions.question: To whom does the Quran describe Muhammad ﷺ as Allah's Messenger in this verse?

options.text: Only one wealthy family
Only people who already speak Arabic
Only the people of one street
All people

questions.explanation: The verse addresses humanity with the Prophet's ﷺ message. Learning Islam is not reserved for a particular language or ancestry.

questions.question: Who possesses knowledge of the unseen independently, without needing anyone to teach Him?

options.text: Allah alone
Every person who guesses confidently
Anyone with many online followers
Anyone who sells a lucky prediction

questions.explanation: Allah alone independently knows the unseen. Messengers know what He chooses to reveal; confident guesses do not become revelation.

questions.question: What does the Quran say about the scales on the Day of Judgment?

options.text: They favor the wealthiest family
They express perfect justice; no one will be wronged
They ignore whatever people do quietly
They measure only a person's popularity

questions.explanation: The verse describes just scales and complete fairness. Allah's judgment does not depend on a crowd's attention or approval.

questions.question: In this Quranic promise of Paradise, which two qualities are mentioned together?

options.text: Wealth and fame
Height and strength
Belief and righteous deeds
Ancestry and expensive clothing

questions.explanation: The verse promises Gardens to those who believe and do good. It gives hope without letting us decide a particular person's final destiny.

questions.question: What do the final verses of Az-Zalzalah teach about small deeds?

options.text: Only actions seen by a crowd can matter
Quiet kindness is always forgotten
Small harmful actions are automatically good
Even very small good and bad deeds matter

questions.explanation: The verses take even tiny deeds seriously. This encourages thoughtful choices, not panic about every passing thought or accidental mistake.

questions.question: What does the hadith emphasize rather than appearance and wealth?

options.text: People's hearts and deeds
People's fashionable belongings
People's family popularity
People's height and hairstyle

questions.explanation: The hadith gives importance to hearts and actions. Outward appearance and possessions do not reveal a person's sincerity.

questions.question: What purpose does Al-Mulk mention in Allah creating life and death?

options.text: Choosing who owns the most toys
Testing which people are best in deeds
Making fame the measure of goodness
Proving every easy life belongs to the best person

questions.explanation: The verse connects life with a test of deeds and describes Allah as Mighty and Forgiving. School marks are not a measure of someone's faith.

questions.question: Which response fits the hadith's guidance when a useful effort has a disappointing outcome?

options.text: Decide that trying was always forbidden
Use the result as permission to harm others
Accept Allah's decree and continue with responsible effort
Assume disappointment proves Allah has rejected us

questions.explanation: The report joins useful effort, seeking Allah's help and accepting His decree. A setback is not proof that a learner is worthless.

questions.question: What does the Quran's instruction to cooperate in goodness show about ordinary human help?

options.text: Seeking any human help is always forbidden
Only working alone can ever be righteous
Every request for help is an act of worship
People can help one another with good actions

questions.explanation: The verse encourages cooperation in good. Asking a teacher for suitable help is different from offering that teacher worship.

questions.question: Does belief in Allah alone complete the entire six-part answer about iman in Jibril's hadith?

options.text: No, the report also names five other foundations
Yes, the other foundations are unrelated to faith
Yes, angels and messengers are only optional guesses
No, because possessions replace belief in Allah

questions.explanation: The report teaches belief in Allah together with angels, scriptures, messengers, the Last Day and decree. We learn the whole answer, not just one part.

questions.question: Does ihsan require an audience of people to make worship meaningful?

options.text: Yes, unseen worship has no meaning
No, awareness of Allah matters even without an audience
Yes, applause is the measure of devotion
No, because worship should never involve attention or care

questions.explanation: Ihsan directs our attention to Allah, who sees us. Other people's presence is not what gives sincere worship its purpose.

questions.question: Does the phrase five pillars mean Islam is literally a building with five stone posts?

options.text: Yes, it names five physical posts everyone must buy
Yes, only people inside one building can be Muslims
No, it describes central foundations of the religion
No, it means five prizes for finishing a quiz

questions.explanation: The hadith uses foundations to explain central parts of Islam. It does not make faith depend on owning a particular building.

questions.question: Does the hadith about branches of faith separate faith from every useful action?

options.text: Yes, practical care is always unrelated to faith
Yes, only impressive speeches can express faith
No, because every dangerous act must be attempted alone
No, it includes removing harm from a path

questions.explanation: The report includes a practical good action among faith's branches. Learning belief can shape safe, considerate conduct as well as words.

questions.question: If two people give similar gifts, must their purposes automatically be identical?

options.text: No, similar actions can have different intentions
Yes, matching gifts always prove matching hearts
Yes, we can read intentions from a price tag
No, because every gift must have a bad purpose

questions.explanation: The hadith gives intentions importance. We can examine our own purpose without pretending to know another person's hidden motives.

questions.question: Does a famous family name automatically prove greater honor before Allah?

options.text: Yes, ancestry replaces righteous conduct
No, the verse emphasizes righteousness rather than family status
Yes, popularity reveals every person's hidden faith
No, because every famous person must lack righteousness

questions.explanation: The verse points to taqwa, not social rank. It neither makes fame proof of goodness nor lets us condemn everyone who is well known.

questions.question: Does another family member's wrongdoing automatically become an innocent person's sin?

options.text: Yes, everyone inherits every relative's sin
Yes, sharing a surname proves personal guilt
No, moral blame is not inherited through family membership
No, because nobody is responsible for their own choices

questions.explanation: The verse rejects carrying another person's burden of sin. This does not excuse our own wrongdoing or responsibility for harm we encourage.

questions.question: Does hope in Allah's forgiveness mean choosing to continue hurting others without concern?

options.text: Yes, mercy makes every harmful choice acceptable
Yes, repentance means planning to repeat the wrong
No, because asking forgiveness is always pointless
No, hope belongs with sincerely turning back

questions.explanation: The invitation to hope is followed by an invitation to return to Allah. Mercy encourages change rather than treating harm as unimportant.

questions.question: Does honoring angels mean treating them as gods beside Allah?

options.text: No, they remain His honored servants
Yes, every honored being deserves worship
Yes, obedience to Allah makes angels divine
No, because angels have no place in Islamic belief

questions.explanation: The verses describe honored servants acting at Allah's command. Respect and belief do not turn a created servant into a god.

questions.question: If a fictional story calls Iblis a fallen angel, which description should an Islamic lesson follow?

options.text: The story's version because it sounds dramatic
The Quran's statement that he was of the jinn
Whichever description is repeated most often
A new identity invented for each lesson

questions.explanation: The Quran identifies Iblis as one of the jinn. An entertaining story is not a source for changing that teaching.

questions.question: Does the Quran's mention of earlier scriptures mean Allah sent no revelation before Muhammad ﷺ?

options.text: Yes, all earlier prophets lacked any revelation
Yes, earlier scriptures are only school notebooks
No, it refers to earlier revelation associated with Ibrahim and Musa
No, because every ordinary book is divine revelation

questions.explanation: The verses name earlier scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa. Belief in revelation includes what Allah sent before the Quran.

questions.question: Does needing an English or Bangla explanation put someone outside the people addressed by the Prophet's ﷺ message?

options.text: Yes, only native Arabic speakers are addressed
Yes, learning a translation makes the message unrelated
No, because the message belongs only to wealthy families
No, the message is for all people

questions.explanation: The verse describes a message to humanity. People can learn its meaning with suitable language support without changing whom the message addresses.

questions.question: Is a confident prediction automatically equal to knowledge Allah reveals to a messenger?

options.text: No, guessing is different from revelation
Yes, confidence turns guesses into divine knowledge
Yes, popularity makes every prediction certain
No, because Allah cannot reveal anything to messengers

questions.explanation: Allah independently knows the unseen and may disclose what He wills to messengers. A person's confident claim is not proof of such knowledge.

questions.question: Do the just scales described in the Quran depend on someone's fame?

options.text: Yes, famous people decide how every deed is weighed
No, Allah's judgment is just rather than popularity based
Yes, an unknown person's deeds can never be considered
No, because the verse says fairness is impossible

questions.explanation: The verse assures complete justice, including what seems very small. Public attention is not the measure of Allah's fairness.

questions.question: Does a prestigious surname replace belief and good deeds in this promise of Paradise?

options.text: Yes, a surname is all the verse requires
Yes, family fame makes personal conduct irrelevant
No, the verse mentions belief and righteous deeds
No, because the verse offers no hope at all

questions.explanation: The promise joins belief with good deeds. It teaches hopeful direction rather than a competition over family names.

questions.question: Does a harmful choice stop mattering merely because nobody else noticed it?

options.text: Yes, unnoticed actions have no significance
Yes, only public mistakes can ever matter
No, because every unnoticed action is automatically harmful
No, the verses teach that even small deeds matter

questions.explanation: The verses encourage care about small good and bad actions. Being unseen by people does not make a deliberate harmful choice harmless.

questions.question: Can expensive clothing alone prove that someone has a more sincere heart?

options.text: No, appearance does not reveal sincerity
Yes, a price tag measures a person's faith
Yes, fashionable clothes guarantee righteous deeds
No, because everyone with nice clothes must be insincere

questions.explanation: The hadith emphasizes hearts and deeds rather than appearance and wealth. Neither admiration nor suspicion about clothing reveals what is in a heart.

questions.question: Does describing life as a test mean a school quiz score measures someone's faith?

options.text: Yes, every full mark guarantees the best faith
No, academic scores do not measure a person's faith
Yes, a low score proves rejection by Allah
No, because good actions have no place in the verse

questions.explanation: The verse concerns the test of deeds, not a classroom ranking of faith. We should learn without judging a child's worth from marks.

questions.question: Does believing in Allah's decree mean refusing to learn from an avoidable mistake?

options.text: Yes, decree makes all future effort pointless
Yes, we must blame others for every setback
No, responsible improvement can go with accepting the outcome
No, because accepting an outcome forbids asking Allah for help

questions.explanation: The hadith encourages useful effort and seeking Allah's help. Accepting what happened does not prevent taking better steps next time.

questions.question: Does asking a teacher to explain a lesson automatically mean worshipping that teacher?

options.text: Yes, every request to a person is worship
Yes, learning requires never accepting human assistance
No, because every form of cooperation is always good
No, ordinary help with good is different from worship

questions.explanation: The verse encourages cooperation in goodness while rejecting cooperation in wrongdoing. Suitable human help is not the same as offering someone worship.

questions.question: A worksheet lists Allah, angels, scriptures, messengers and the Last Day. Which foundation from Jibril's answer is missing?

options.text: Belief in divine decree, concerning good and bad
Owning a particular kind of clothing
Being praised by every teacher
Belonging to the most famous family

questions.explanation: The hadith's answer includes divine decree as well as the five foundations already listed. Learn the complete set without treating it as a popularity ranking.

questions.question: You practice worship quietly without anyone praising you. Which thought reflects ihsan?

options.text: Without applause, worship has no purpose
Allah sees me, so I should worship with care
Only my teacher can give worship meaning
I should care only if a camera is recording

questions.explanation: Ihsan connects careful worship with awareness of Allah. Quiet practice does not need a public audience to matter.

questions.question: A class poster has four pillars: shahadah, salah, zakat and Ramadan fasting. Which pillar completes the list?

options.text: Collecting trophies
Speaking several languages
Hajj
Owning a large house

questions.explanation: Hajj is included in the hadith's five foundations. Learning the list is different from requiring a child to travel immediately.

questions.question: An adult safely removes something blocking a walkway. Which belief lesson helps explain the act's value?

options.text: Faith concerns only what people say in a quiz
Helping walkers can never connect with faith
A useful action matters only if filmed
Removing harm from a path is a branch of faith

questions.explanation: The hadith includes removing harm among faith's branches. Children should ask an adult about dangerous objects rather than handling them alone.

questions.question: Two classmates share supplies. One wants to help; another only wants applause. Which lesson applies?

options.text: Similar visible actions can have different intentions
Matching supplies prove their intentions are identical
Only the supplies' price can explain their purpose
The loudest applause proves the most sincere heart

questions.explanation: The scenario illustrates why intentions matter. In real life, examine your own purpose rather than claiming to read someone else's heart.

questions.question: A child says their famous surname automatically makes them better before Allah. Which reminder fits the Quran?

options.text: A surname always measures hidden sincerity
The verse values taqwa rather than family prestige
Fame replaces every need for good conduct
Only children from unknown families can be righteous

questions.explanation: The verse connects honor with righteousness, not ancestry. It teaches humility without asking children to rank other people's faith.

questions.question: Someone blames an innocent child for a cousin's wrongdoing only because they share a family. Which principle applies?

options.text: A shared family name proves personal guilt
Every cousin automatically shares every action
One person does not carry another person's sin
Innocent people must take blame to be polite

questions.explanation: The verse teaches that another person's burden of sin is not inherited. A child should not be shamed merely for a relative's conduct.

questions.question: After behaving unkindly, Sara thinks improving is pointless because Allah's mercy cannot reach her. What should she remember?

options.text: One mistake permanently ends every hope
Mercy means she should plan more harm
Only other people's compliments can permit repentance
Do not despair; turn back to Allah and seek improvement

questions.explanation: The verses invite hope in Allah's mercy and sincere return. Sara can seek forgiveness and learn to treat people better.

questions.question: A lesson says angels obey Allah, so they must also be gods. Which correction is sound?

options.text: Obeying Allah does not make His servants divine
Every obedient servant becomes a god
Angels make Allah follow their commands
The Quran says angels deserve worship beside Allah

questions.explanation: The verses describe angels as honored servants acting at Allah's command. Their obedience does not make them partners in His divinity.

questions.question: A quiz card says, "Iblis was one of the jinn." Should the card be changed just to match a fantasy film?

options.text: Yes, fantasy films decide Islamic belief
No, the card matches the Quran's statement
Yes, the most dramatic version must be true
No, because every film detail is revelation

questions.explanation: Islamic teaching follows the Quran's identification of Iblis. Fictional entertainment does not determine what we believe about him.

questions.question: A friend thinks there were no earlier scriptures before the Quran. Which pair named in Al-Ala helps correct this?

options.text: Two modern school textbooks
Two poetry books written this year
The scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa
Two notebooks with no connection to revelation

questions.explanation: Al-Ala mentions earlier scriptures associated with Ibrahim and Musa. This supports learning about revelation before the Quran without inventing extra details.

questions.question: Lina worries the Prophet's ﷺ message is not for her because she speaks Bangla at home. Which reply fits the verse?

options.text: Only native Arabic speakers are addressed
Her home language makes learning Islam impossible
Only one nationality can study the message
His message addresses all people, including different language communities

questions.explanation: The Quran describes Muhammad ﷺ as a messenger to all people. Language support can help Lina understand a message that includes her.

questions.question: An online account claims it independently knows every person's future. Which reminder fits Islamic belief?

options.text: Complete independent knowledge of the unseen belongs to Allah
Many followers make the account all-knowing
Charging money proves its claims are revelation
Confident speech makes every future claim certain

questions.explanation: A claim to know the unseen is not proved by confidence or popularity. Ask a trusted adult instead of relying on such predictions.

questions.question: A classmate thinks Allah's judgment favors popular people. What does the verse about scales teach instead?

options.text: The biggest audience decides every judgment
Allah establishes just scales and wrongs no one
Unknown people's actions are never considered
Popularity can replace fairness

questions.explanation: The verse promises complete justice, even concerning very small deeds. It offers reassurance that Allah does not judge by popularity.

questions.question: A worksheet asks what the verse's promise of Gardens mentions. Which answer should you select?

options.text: Having the most famous surname
Owning the most costly belongings
Believing and doing righteous deeds
Winning every classroom competition

questions.explanation: The verse joins belief and good deeds in its promise. The question concerns the teaching, not judging any particular child's final destiny.

questions.question: A friend says a small kindness is worthless because nobody noticed. Which response fits Az-Zalzalah?

options.text: Only actions with a photograph count
Unnoticed kindness is always wasted
Small actions have no place in belief
Even very small good deeds matter

questions.explanation: The verses give weight to even tiny deeds. A small kindness need not become public to be worth doing.

questions.question: Children rank each other's faith by the price of their clothes. Which reminder follows the hadith?

options.text: Allah gives importance to hearts and deeds, not price tags
The most expensive clothes prove the best heart
Every plain outfit proves perfect sincerity
A person's faith can be read from their hairstyle

questions.explanation: The hadith turns attention toward hearts and actions. Clothing does not give children a way to measure another person's faith.

questions.question: A learner gets a low school mark and says, "This proves I have no worth before Allah." Which correction is helpful?

options.text: Every low mark proves rejection by Allah
School marks do not measure faith; keep learning and doing good
Only top students can ever do good deeds
A quiz result reveals someone's final destiny

questions.explanation: The verse concerns life's test of deeds. Support the learner's improvement without confusing academic performance with their faith or worth.

questions.question: Yusuf's project goes wrong because he skipped a step. What combines accepting Allah's decree with responsibility?

options.text: Say decree means learning from mistakes is forbidden
Blame a classmate who was not involved
Accept the outcome, correct the step and try again
Give up every useful effort permanently

questions.explanation: The hadith encourages beneficial effort and seeking Allah's help. Accepting an outcome can go with taking responsibility and improving a plan.

questions.question: You make dua, then ask your teacher for help understanding a lesson. How should these actions be understood?

options.text: Asking a teacher automatically means worshipping them
Making dua forbids learning from other people
Every form of dependence on any person is divine worship
Suitable human help can go with turning to Allah

questions.explanation: The Quran encourages cooperation in good. Learning with a teacher is ordinary assistance, while worship remains directed to Allah.
